label: Japanese Economic Miracle
pitch:
Postwar Japan (1945–1991) reinvented itself from atomic rubble into the world's second-largest economy in roughly thirty years, then watched it all freeze in a deflationary haze for thirty more.

🔑 Key Facts:
• The Yoshida Doctrine traded military autonomy for the American security umbrella, freeing Japan to focus all resources on economic growth
• Ikeda Hayato's Income Doubling Plan promised to double national income in ten years — Japan did it in seven
• The Toyota Production System reinvented global manufacturing with just-in-time logistics and kaizen continuous improvement
• At the 1989 bubble peak, the Tokyo Imperial Palace grounds were theoretically worth more than all the real estate in California

🤔 Why It Matters: Japan proved that a defeated, occupied, atomic-bombed country could rebuild into an economic superpower in a single generation, and the developmentalist state model — a strong industrial ministry, lifetime employment, keiretsu networks, mass higher education — became the template every late-twentieth-century Asian miracle would copy.

🎲 Wild Card: At the height of the bubble, Mitsubishi Estate paid $846 million for Rockefeller Center and a Tokyo speculator paid $82 million for a Van Gogh — peak symbolic moments of the only era when the world genuinely believed Japan was about to overtake the United States economically.

spans.label: Allied Occupation
spans.description: Under General MacArthur and the SCAP authority, Japan was demilitarized and democratized: a new constitution renouncing war, sweeping land reform, the dissolution of the zaibatsu, women's suffrage, and the Tokyo war crimes trials. The Korean War procurement boom ended the postwar slump and launched the recovery.

spans.label: Yoshida Doctrine and 1955 System
spans.description: Prime Minister Yoshida Shigeru's strategy of minimal rearmament and total economic focus, combined with the LDP's emergence as the dominant party in 1955, set the political and strategic frame for the high-growth era. The 1960 Anpo crisis tested and confirmed the bargain.

spans.label: High-Growth Era
spans.description: Average annual GDP growth of nearly 10% under MITI's industrial guidance, the keiretsu system, the Toyota Production System, and the salaryman labor model. The 1964 Tokyo Olympics, the Shinkansen, and Expo '70 in Osaka announced the new Japan to the world.

spans.label: Stable Growth and Trade Friction
spans.description: The 1973 oil shock ended the high-growth miracle but Japan adapted faster than any other industrial country, shifting toward energy efficiency and high-value-added exports. The country became 'Japan as Number One,' Toyota and Sony and Honda conquered global markets, and trade friction with the United States grew bitter.

spans.label: The Bubble Years
spans.description: The 1985 Plaza Accord pushed the yen up sharply; the Bank of Japan cut interest rates to support exporters; the resulting flood of cheap credit fueled the largest asset bubble in postwar history. The Nikkei peaked at 38,957 in December 1989; the bubble's collapse over 1990–91 ended the miracle.

events.label: Japan Surrenders
events.description: After atomic bombs destroyed Hiroshima and Nagasaki and the Soviet Union entered the war, Emperor Hirohito broadcast Japan's surrender on August 15, 1945 — most subjects heard his voice for the first time — and the formal capitulation was signed aboard the USS Missouri on September 2.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The Potsdam Declaration had warned Japan of 'prompt and utter destruction' if it didn't surrender unconditionally, but Tokyo initially ignored it. A coup attempt by hardline officers to prevent the surrender broadcast was foiled the night before it aired. Foreign Minister Mamoru Shigemitsu signed the surrender documents in top hat and morning coat — he had lost a leg to an assassination attempt years earlier and walked with a cane.

events.label: MacArthur and SCAP
events.description: General Douglas MacArthur arrived at Atsugi airfield on August 30, 1945 as Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers (SCAP) and governed Japan effectively as a viceroy for nearly six years, running occupation policy through his Tokyo headquarters until President Truman fired him in April 1951 over Korean War strategy.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: MacArthur's decision to land at Atsugi — unarmed, in an unarmed transport, surrounded by Japanese troops who had stopped fighting two weeks earlier — was a theatrical gamble on personal authority that paid off completely. He set up SCAP headquarters in the Dai-Ichi Life Insurance Building directly opposite the Imperial Palace and did not return to the United States at all between 1937 and his dismissal in 1951 — fourteen years.

events.label: Tokyo War Crimes Trials
events.description: The International Military Tribunal for the Far East tried 28 senior Japanese military and civilian leaders for crimes against peace, war crimes, and crimes against humanity from April 1946 to November 1948, sentencing seven — including wartime Prime Minister Tojo Hideki — to death by hanging.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The tribunal was modeled directly on the Nuremberg trials running simultaneously in Germany. Emperor Hirohito was deliberately left off the indictment list at MacArthur's insistence — Australia and the Soviet Union had wanted him tried, and American public opinion after Pearl Harbor and Bataan would have supported execution. Two defendants died during the proceedings; one was found mentally unfit to stand trial.

events.label: Emperor's Humanity Declaration
events.description: On New Year's Day 1946, Emperor Hirohito issued the Ningen Sengen ('Humanity Declaration'), explicitly renouncing the doctrine that he was a living god — collapsing the State Shinto theology built around imperial divinity and recasting the emperor as a constitutional symbol of national unity with no political power.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The declaration was drafted in close consultation with SCAP, not by Japanese officials alone. It opened with a quote from the Five Charter Oath of 1868 — the foundational Meiji-era reform pledge — tying the new postwar order rhetorically to the Meiji legacy rather than presenting it as foreign imposition. The Japanese word the declaration used to deny divinity, akitsumikami, was an archaic term so obscure that many ordinary Japanese had never encountered it.

events.label: 1947 Constitution and Article 9
events.description: Japan's 1947 constitution — drafted in roughly a week by a small SCAP team under Brigadier General Courtney Whitney after the Japanese government's own draft was rejected as too close to the prewar Meiji constitution — established parliamentary democracy, a ceremonial emperor, women's suffrage, and the renunciation of war.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The SCAP team that wrote the draft included at least one staffer, Beate Sirota Gordon, who was 22 years old at the time and personally inserted the women's rights provisions based on her reading of other national constitutions. The document was written in English, translated into Japanese, and then presented to the existing Meiji-era Diet for ratification — technically making a foreign-imposed constitution a domestic Japanese legislative act. Every postwar Japanese government has had the legal authority to amend it and has chosen not to.

events.label: Article 9
events.description: Article 9 of Japan's 1947 constitution renounces war as a sovereign right and bans the maintenance of any military force — the only clause of its kind in any major national constitution. Governments have worked around it since 1954 by classifying the Self-Defense Forces as non-'war potential,' but the article itself has never been formally amended.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The clause was drafted during the American occupation specifically to prevent Japanese rearmament, following the same logic the Allies had tried (and failed) with Germany after World War I. Despite decades of LDP pressure for amendment, every formal revision attempt has stalled against a combination of coalition partner resistance and consistent supermajority public opposition. The legal fiction of 'purely defensive' forces means Japan today operates destroyers, fighter jets, and amphibious units that most countries would call a military — all technically constitutional.

events.label: Land Reform
events.description: SCAP's 1947–49 land reform forced absentee landlords to sell tenant-farmed land to the government at fixed prices, which resold it to the tenant cultivators on low-interest credit — converting roughly 90% of tenant farmers into owner-occupiers and eliminating the rural landlord class that had been a prewar conservative power base.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Before the reform, roughly 30% of agricultural land was worked by tenants paying rents that often consumed half the harvest. The reform was more radical than anything SCAP attempted in continental Europe at the same time. It also aligned with American Cold War strategy: the Chinese Communist Party was winning its civil war partly on promises of land redistribution, and a Japan with contented small-farmer owners was less vulnerable to the same appeal.

events.label: Zaibatsu Dissolution
events.description: SCAP's Holding Company Liquidation Commission broke up the four great zaibatsu — Mitsui, Mitsubishi, Sumitomo, Yasuda — that had controlled Japan's wartime industrial economy, dissolving holding companies, stripping founding families of controlling stakes, and enacting antitrust laws modeled on American Sherman and Clayton Acts.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Zaibatsu means roughly 'financial clique' — each was a family-owned holding company at the top, with a major bank, a trading company, and dozens of industrial subsidiaries beneath it. The Iwasaki family (Mitsubishi), the Mitsui family, and the Sumitomo family never regained operational control after dissolution. The same industrial groups rebuilt as keiretsu (horizontally networked firms sharing a bank) once Cold War politics shifted American priorities from dismantlement to Japanese economic strength.

events.label: Women's Suffrage
events.description: Japanese women voted for the first time in the April 1946 general election; 39 women won seats in the Diet (8.4% of the lower house), a share that would not be reached again until 2017, and the right to vote was enshrined in the 1947 constitution alongside equal property and divorce rights.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Voter turnout among newly enfranchised women in that first election reached roughly 67% — higher than many established democracies see in routine elections. The franchise extension actually covered all Japanese over 20, not just women; the prewar system had restricted voting to men over 25 who paid a minimum tax. Japanese feminist organizations had been demanding suffrage since the 1920s, and women's groups that had been suppressed under wartime mobilization reconstituted almost immediately after surrender.

events.label: Dodge Line
events.description: Detroit banker Joseph Dodge, sent by the Truman administration in early 1949, imposed an austerity program on Japan that a Japanese government could never have forced through politically: balanced budget, end of industrial subsidies, and a single fixed exchange rate of 360 yen to the dollar that crushed hyperinflation — and accidentally anchored Japanese export competitiveness for the next twenty-two years.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Before the Dodge Line, Japan had been running multiple exchange rates under occupation management; Dodge collapsed them all to a single 360-yen peg. The immediate shock produced a sharp recession and wave of industrial layoffs through 1949 — but the undervalued rate made Japanese exports so cheap on world markets that when the Korean War orders hit in 1950, the economy had a perfectly primed export engine waiting. Dodge's austerity was the last thing SCAP imposed, and arguably the most consequential economic decision of the occupation.

events.label: Korean War Procurement Boom
events.description: When North Korea crossed the 38th parallel on June 25, 1950, Japan became the United Nations command's primary supply base and repair depot, generating roughly $2.3 billion in special procurement orders (tokuju) that doubled Japanese industrial production between 1949 and 1951 — the economic shock that ended the Dodge Line recession and launched the high-growth era.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The textile sector, steel industry, and engineering workshops were essentially rebuilt at American military expense. Prime Minister Yoshida Shigeru reportedly called the Korean War kami no tasuke — 'a gift from the gods' — though the phrase appears in colleagues' accounts rather than his own writings. The asymmetry was stark: Korea lost three million people in the war; Japan, eight years after its own catastrophic defeat that killed roughly the same number, profited from the same conflict.

events.label: Treaty of San Francisco
events.description: Signed on September 8, 1951 and effective April 28, 1952, the Treaty of San Francisco formally ended the occupation and restored Japanese sovereignty, with Japan renouncing all claims to Korea, Taiwan, the Kuriles, southern Sakhalin, and its former Pacific island mandates — though the Soviet Union and China didn't sign, leaving major territorial disputes formally unresolved.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Italy and both claimant Chinese governments were excluded from the conference entirely, and Korea was not invited due to disagreement over which Korean government was legitimate — North or South. The Northern Territories (four islands Russia has held since 1945) remain unresolved to this day, meaning Japan and Russia have never signed a formal peace treaty ending World War II. The occupation that ended was one of the most transformative in modern history: in under seven years, American authority had remade Japan's constitution, land ownership, industrial structure, and military.

events.label: U.S.-Japan Security Treaty
events.description: The U.S.-Japan Security Treaty (Anpo, short for Anzen Hosho Joyaku) signed the same day as the peace treaty permitted American forces to remain indefinitely in Japan and committed both nations to mutual defense — terms so favorable to the United States that the 1960 revision triggered the largest mass protests in postwar Japanese history.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The original 1951 treaty gave American commanders authority to deploy forces from Japanese bases without Japanese government approval and placed American servicemen accused of crimes against Japanese civilians under American rather than Japanese jurisdiction — a partial restoration of the 'extraterritoriality' the Meiji government had spent decades fighting to abolish from unequal 19th-century treaties. The 1960 revision reduced but did not eliminate these asymmetries. American bases, most controversially on Okinawa, remain politically contentious; Okinawa hosts about 70% of U.S. military facilities in Japan despite comprising less than 1% of the country's land area.

events.label: Yoshida Shigeru
events.description: Yoshida Shigeru (1878–1967) was the career diplomat who served as prime minister through most of the American occupation and set the strategic direction that defined Japanese policy for the next forty years — minimum rearmament, the American security umbrella, and an all-in bet on economic growth.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Yoshida had been briefly imprisoned by the Kempeitai (wartime military police) in April 1945 for suspected involvement in back-channel peace efforts — which gave him impeccable democratic credentials with both the occupation authorities and the Japanese public when the war ended. He was famous for withering sarcasm in both Japanese and English, and occupation staff who tried to dictate policy to him privately endured it; SCAP's own nickname for him was "One Man Yoshida." He governed until age seventy-six, wearing three-piece suits with watch chains and keeping a famous British bulldog named Lord.

events.label: Yoshida Doctrine
events.description: The Yoshida Doctrine was postwar Japan's core strategic formula: accept the American military alliance and constitutional pacifism, spend as little as possible on defense (roughly 1% of GDP), and direct everything else toward economic reconstruction and growth.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The term 'Yoshida Doctrine' was actually coined decades after Yoshida left office — he was too cagey to ever articulate it in a single document, and some scholars argue it is more a retrospective label than a conscious plan. The economic payoff was mathematical: Japan spent ~1% of GDP on defense through the high-growth era, against ~6–7% for the United States and ~3–4% for West Germany; over thirty years of compounding, that gap represents an enormous accumulated investment advantage. Historian Kenneth Pyle compared it to Bismarck's Realpolitik — a set of practical principles for maximizing national interest through strategic restraint rather than military posturing.

events.label: Self-Defense Forces Established
events.description: The Japan Self-Defense Forces (JSDF), established in July 1954, grew from the 75,000-strong National Police Reserve MacArthur ordered in 1950 when American troops deployed to Korea — organized as three branches (ground, maritime, air) under the legal fiction that purely defensive forces did not violate Article 9's prohibition on armed forces.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The JSDF is controlled by the Ministry of Defense with the Prime Minister as commander-in-chief, an arrangement designed to prevent any recurrence of the prewar military autonomy from civilian government. Restrictions on overseas deployment held until 1992, when JSDF engineers deployed to Cambodia under a UN peacekeeping mission — the first deployment outside Japan since 1945. By the 2020s Japan had announced plans to double its defense budget to 2% of GDP, the most significant rearmament shift in the postwar era.

events.label: 1955 System
events.description: The '1955 System' is the name for the political order created when Japan's two main conservative parties merged into the Liberal Democratic Party in November 1955 — a one-party-dominant democracy in which the LDP governed nearly uninterrupted for the next thirty-eight years and real competition happened inside the party's factions rather than between parties.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The term was coined by political scientist Junnosuke Masumi, who called the 1955 system 'a grand political dam into which the history of Japanese politics surge.' The Japan Socialist Party reunified at exactly the same moment as its main opposition role, cementing the one-and-a-half-party structure. The LDP's electoral ceiling of roughly 45–55% of the vote was consistently enough for a majority in Japan's single-member district system, which amplified the dominant-party effect. The two brief breaks in LDP rule — 1993–94 and 2009–12 — both ended with the LDP returning to power.

events.label: Liberal Democratic Party
events.description: The Liberal Democratic Party (Jiminto) formed in November 1955 by merging the Liberal and Democratic parties, has governed Japan almost continuously ever since — the longest unbroken run of single-party dominance in any major postwar democracy.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The LDP was less a unified party than a federation of competing factions, each with its own informal headquarters, funding networks, and preferred ministers — the Yoshida-Ikeda-Tanaka line and the Kishi-Fukuda line being the two main genealogies. Premiership rotated among faction leaders rather than being determined by a single internal primary, which gave the party a self-renewal mechanism that most dominant parties lack. As of 2025 Sanae Takaichi heads the party, leading a coalition with the Japan Innovation Party — the first woman to hold the LDP presidency.

events.label: 1960 Anpo Protests
events.description: The Anpo protests of 1959–60 were the largest mass demonstrations in Japanese history, erupting over the renewal of the U.S.-Japan Security Treaty ('Anpo' is shorthand for the Japanese term for Security Treaty) — 30 million signed petitions, hundreds of thousands surrounded the Diet, and one student was killed before Prime Minister Kishi rammed ratification through and resigned.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The protests also flared again in 1970 at the treaty's next renewal, though less violently. President Eisenhower's state visit in June 1960 had to be cancelled after his press secretary's motorcade was mobbed at Haneda Airport — a humiliation with no real Cold War precedent among US allies. Kishi's political toxicity stemmed partly from his wartime past: he had served as Tojo's commerce and munitions minister and spent three years in Sugamo Prison as a Class A war crimes suspect before being released without trial in 1948. His political defeat over Anpo effectively closed the door on constitutional revision and major rearmament for a generation.

events.label: MITI
events.description: The Ministry of International Trade and Industry (MITI), assembled in 1949 from the wartime Munitions Ministry, was the institutional brain of Japanese industrial policy — directing investment through low-interest loans, foreign-currency licensing, technology-import approvals, and informal 'administrative guidance' (gyosei shido) that firms ignored at their regulatory peril.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: MITI's record was genuinely mixed: it helped build the world's most efficient large-scale steel industry and captured half the global shipbuilding market by 1960, but it also tried — and failed — to force Honda to merge with Toyota, and its protection of mainframe-oriented Japanese computer firms left them steamrolled by American PC architectures in the 1980s. Chalmers Johnson's 1982 book MITI and the Japanese Miracle made the ministry famous to Western audiences; subsequent economists argued MITI was riding a wave it had not itself created. MITI was folded into the new Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry (METI) in 2001.

events.label: Keiretsu System
events.description: Keiretsu (interlocking corporate networks) replaced the dissolved zaibatsu conglomerates and dominated the postwar Japanese economy — six major horizontal groups (Mitsubishi, Mitsui, Sumitomo, Fuyo, Sanwa, Daiichi-Kangyo) each centered on a main bank, a trading company, and dozens of cross-shareholding manufacturing affiliates, plus separate vertical keiretsu organized around a single assembling firm like Toyota.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The cross-shareholding structure made hostile takeovers nearly impossible: member firms held each other's stock for the long term and had no incentive to sell to an outside acquirer. Banks lent to keiretsu affiliates at preferential rates and rolled loans over indefinitely, enabling the aggressive long-term capacity investment — steel mills, shipyards, semiconductor fabs — that short-term-focused American or European firms would not have funded. This became a structural liability after the 1990s asset-price collapse, when those rolled-over loans turned into mountains of non-performing debt.

events.label: Deming Prize
events.description: The Deming Prize, established in 1951 by the Japanese Union of Scientists and Engineers, honored W. Edwards Deming — the American statistician whose postwar lectures on statistical quality control transformed Japanese manufacturing and whose methods trace directly to the kaizen culture that became Japan's manufacturing signature.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Deming's methods — sampling-based quality assessment, continuous improvement, worker involvement in quality decisions — were standard American operations research that American manufacturers had largely ignored, because high postwar profit margins made quality investment seem unnecessary. The awards ceremony has been broadcast on Japanese national television every year since 1951. The prize eventually opened to non-Japanese companies and has been won by firms in India, the United States, and Thailand.

events.label: Toyota Production System
events.description: The Toyota Production System (TPS), developed by engineer Ohno Taiichi at Toyota between the late 1940s and the 1970s, combined just-in-time inventory (parts arrive exactly when needed), jidoka (any worker can stop the line for a defect), and kaizen (continuous improvement by frontline workers) — enabling Toyota to produce a high-quality vehicle with roughly one-third the labor hours of American manufacturers.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Ohno developed just-in-time partly by studying American supermarket restocking — the idea that shelves should be replenished based on what customers actually take, not on centralized forecasting. His 1978 book Toyota Production System: Beyond Large-Scale Production brought the method to international audiences; by 2000, 'lean manufacturing' — the Western generalization of Ohno's principles — was the standard model for industrial production worldwide, applied everywhere from Boeing to hospitals.

events.label: Sony Transistor Radio
events.description: Sony (then Tokyo Tsushin Kogyo) released the TR-55 in 1955, Japan's first commercial transistor radio — a pocket-sized device built on a transistor patent licensed from Bell Labs for $25,000, and the first Japanese consumer product to win mass acceptance in the American market.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: AT&T's lawyers had concluded the $25,000 licensing fee wasn't worth fighting over — a miscalculation that gave Japan's entire consumer-electronics industry its launching pad. The company renamed itself Sony in 1958 (a portmanteau of sonus, Latin for sound, and sonny, the American affectionate term for a young boy) and through the 1960s released the Trinitron color television (1968) and the first portable cassette recorder (1962), establishing Japan as the global consumer-electronics leader.

events.label: Sony Walkman
events.description: The Sony Walkman TPS-L2, released in July 1979, was a portable cassette player with no recording function — a deliberately stripped-down product that Sony's own sales team predicted would flop. Co-founder Morita Akio pushed it through anyway. It sold over 200 million units across all variants, transformed everyday music listening from a stationary to a mobile experience, and gave Japan its first globally iconic consumer-electronics product.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Morita carried a prototype everywhere for weeks before launch, demonstrating it to anyone who would listen — he was convinced people would pay for the ability to hear music while moving through the world even if they couldn't record anything. The original model came with two headphone jacks and a 'hotline' button that let users briefly mute the music to have a conversation — that feature was quietly dropped after a few months when it turned out buyers never used it. The brand name was a deliberate fusion of 'walk' and the then-popular suffix '-man' (from 'Pressman,' an earlier Sony recorder).

events.label: Honda Motor
events.description: Honda Motor Company, founded in October 1948 by self-taught engineer Honda Soichiro, started by bolting surplus army engines onto bicycles and became the world's largest motorcycle manufacturer by 1959, then entered automobile production in 1963 — famously defying MITI's attempt to force it to merge with Toyota.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Honda is the only major Japanese automaker that MITI failed to absorb into a consolidated corporate structure — Honda Soichiro simply refused, and the ministry backed down. Honda's entry into the U.S. motorcycle market in the early 1960s used the now-famous 'You meet the nicest people on a Honda' campaign, which deliberately targeted everyday American consumers rather than the tough-guy image motorcycles then carried, transforming the entire U.S. motorcycle market.

events.label: Honda Civic
events.description: The first-generation Honda Civic, released in July 1972, was a small front-wheel-drive subcompact designed specifically for the U.S. market — low fuel consumption, modest interior, low maintenance cost. It arrived just fifteen months before the oil shock hit, perfectly positioned: American consumers abandoning big-engine Detroit cars flooded into the Civic and Toyota Corolla, and within a decade Japanese automakers held over 20% of the U.S. market.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The Civic's CVCC engine — Honda's Compound Vortex Controlled Combustion design — met the U.S. Clean Air Act of 1970 without a catalytic converter, something the Big Three insisted was technically impossible. Honda proved it wasn't, in 1975, which was a serious embarrassment for Detroit's lobbying position. As of 2021, over 27 million Civics have been sold across all generations, making it one of the best-selling car models in history.

events.label: Honda Soichiro
events.description: Honda Soichiro (1906–1991) founded Honda Motor in 1948 — starting by attaching war-surplus engines to bicycles in a wooden shack — and built it into a global automotive and motorcycle manufacturer before stepping down as president in October 1973. Famously hands-on, publicly eccentric, and contemptuous of bureaucratic ceremony, he refused to hand the company to his son, breaking the custom that other founding families followed, and the company has been run by professional managers ever since.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Honda's path into automobiles was officially blocked by MITI in the early 1960s — the ministry had decided Japan had enough car companies and told Honda to stick to motorcycles. Honda ignored the directive, launched the S500 sports car in 1963, and was never penalized, which revealed both the limits of MITI's authority and Honda's unusually combative stance toward government guidance. He was the first Japanese industrialist inducted into the Automotive Hall of Fame (1989).

events.label: Morita Akio
events.description: Morita Akio (1921–1999), co-founder of Sony with engineer Ibuka Masaru, was the public face of Japanese consumer electronics in the United States — charming, fluent in English, and deeply embedded in American business and social circles. He moved his family to New York in 1963 to Americanize Sony's brand, championed the Walkman over internal opposition, and in 1989 co-authored 'The Japan That Can Say No' with nationalist politician Ishihara Shintaro, a polemic that alarmed Washington and complicated Sony's American relationships.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Morita was unusual among Japanese executives of his era in socializing extensively with American CEOs, politicians, and celebrities — he played tennis with Henry Kissinger and socialized with entertainment executives in ways that made Sony's American acquisitions (CBS Records in 1988, Columbia Pictures in 1989) feel like relationship deals as much as financial ones. He suffered a stroke while playing tennis in 1993 and, incapacitated, watched from the sidelines as the Columbia acquisition turned into a billion-dollar write-down.

events.label: Ikeda Hayato
events.description: Ikeda Hayato (1899–1965) became prime minister in July 1960, inheriting the job from Kishi immediately after the Anpo security crisis, and deliberately turned Japan's political conversation away from constitutional fights toward a single, irresistible promise: your income will double. His 'low posture' style — economic focus, ideological quietude, salaryman appeal — set the template for LDP governance for a generation.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Ikeda had spent his early career as a Finance Ministry tax bureaucrat — not a politician by origin — and it was this technocratic background that gave him credibility when making big economic promises. He resigned the prime ministership in November 1964, days after the Tokyo Olympics closing ceremony, after being diagnosed with throat cancer; he died nine months later at sixty-five, having watched his signature plan succeed ahead of schedule.

events.label: Income Doubling Plan
events.description: Announced in December 1960, the Income Doubling Plan (Shotoku Baizou Keikaku) committed the government to doubling per-capita real income within ten years through infrastructure investment, education spending, and growth-friendly fiscal policy — with the political genius of using bureaucratic forecasts as a national mobilization device.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The plan called for an average annual growth rate of 7.2% to hit its target; Japan actually averaged over 10% per year and doubled the economy in under seven years instead of ten. Its real power was psychological: by framing growth as a national project shared by government, labor, and corporations alike, it displaced the divisive security and constitutional debates that had been tearing Japanese politics apart since 1960.

events.label: 1964 Tokyo Olympics
events.description: The 1964 Summer Olympics, held in Tokyo from October 10–24, were the first Olympics in Asia — and Japan's formal reintroduction to the world as a recovered constitutional democracy rather than the defeated aggressor of 1945, watched globally through the first real-time international satellite television broadcasts.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The opening-ceremony torchbearer was Sakai Yoshinori, nineteen years old and born in Hiroshima on August 6, 1945 — the day of the atomic bombing — a choice of deliberate and unmistakable symbolism. Tokyo had originally been awarded the 1940 Olympics, which were cancelled due to Japan's invasion of China and then World War II; the 1964 games were in that sense a twenty-four-year-delayed debut. Japan finished third in the medal count, behind the U.S. and Soviet Union, winning 16 gold medals.

events.label: Tokaido Shinkansen
events.description: The Tokaido Shinkansen (bullet train) opened on October 1, 1964 — nine days before the Tokyo Olympics — becoming the world's first high-speed rail line, connecting Tokyo and Osaka across 320 miles at up to 130 mph and cutting the journey from six hours to four.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The Shinkansen network has carried over 10 billion passengers without a single fatal accident from train collision or derailment across sixty years of operation — a safety record unmatched by any major transport system in the world. The project's budget roughly doubled from original estimates during construction, a classic megaproject overrun, but the line was still completed on schedule. The map-based leadImage is informational rather than visual, so a more evocative photo candidate is worth noting.

events.label: Tokyo Tower
events.description: Tokyo Tower, completed in December 1958, is a 332.9-meter (1,092-foot) red-and-white lattice broadcast tower in central Tokyo, inspired by — and slightly taller than — the Eiffel Tower, built to carry the new television networks' antennas and quickly adopted as the visual symbol of Tokyo's postwar recovery.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The tower is painted white and international orange (not red as commonly assumed) specifically to comply with air-safety regulations for aircraft visibility. It held the title of tallest structure in Japan until 2012, when the Tokyo Skytree surpassed it at 634 meters. Despite losing its broadcast function as antennas migrated to the Skytree, Tokyo Tower remains one of Japan's most visited tourist sites, receiving some 3 million visitors per year.

events.label: Expo '70 Osaka
events.description: Expo '70 in Osaka ran from March to September 1970 as the first World's Fair held in Asia, drawing 64.2 million visitors — more than half the population of Japan at the time — under the theme 'Progress and Harmony for Mankind,' with the Tower of the Sun by sculptor Okamoto Taro as its lasting visual icon.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Expo '70 was the largest World's Fair in history up to that point by attendance. The site was designed in part by architect Tange Kenzo (who had also designed the Yoyogi gymnasium for the 1964 Olympics), and featured pavilions from 77 countries. Three years after the fair closed, the 1973 oil shock ended the high-growth era that Expo '70 had been celebrating.

events.label: Tange Kenzo and Metabolism
events.description: Tange Kenzo (1913–2005) was Japan's most internationally recognized postwar architect — the designer of the Hiroshima Peace Memorial Park (1955), the Yoyogi National Gymnasium for the 1964 Tokyo Olympics, and the master plan for Osaka Expo '70. He was also the founding patron of the Metabolist movement, which proposed that buildings should function like living organisms: expandable, replaceable, and adaptable over time.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Tange won the Pritzker Prize in 1987, the first Japanese architect to receive architecture's highest honor, which helped establish the international reputation that later allowed Ando Tadao, Isozaki Arata, and others to follow. His Hiroshima Peace Memorial design was deliberately oriented so that the A-Bomb Dome ruins framed through the memorial arch formed a straight line to the epicenter of the bomb — a spatial argument against forgetting. His Tokyo Metropolitan Government Building, completed as the bubble peaked, was nicknamed 'Tocho' by Tokyoites and became one of the city's free public observation decks.
